result.text:
1	Theory
2	======
3	
4	Introduction
5	------------
6	
7	The analysis of homogenous cross-sections is particularly relevant in structural design,
8	in particular for the design of steel structures, where complex built-up sections are
9	often utilised. Accurate warping independent properties, such as the second moment of
10	area and section moduli, are crucial input for structural analysis and stress
11	verification. Warping dependent properties, such as the Saint-Venant torsion constant
12	and warping constant are essential in the verification of slender steel structures when
13	lateral-torsional buckling is critical.
14	
15	Warping independent properties for basic cross-sections are relatively simple to
16	calculate by hand. However accurate warping independent properties, even for the most
17	basic cross-section, require solving several boundary value partial differential
18	equations. This necessitates numerical methods in the calculation of these properties,
19	which can be extended to arbitrary complex sections.
20	
21	This section of the documentation describes the theory and application of the finite
22	element method to cross-sectional analysis used by ``sectionproperties``. The goal of
23	``sectionproperties`` is to perform cross-sectional and stress analysis on arbitrary
24	cross-sections, see below figure. In its simplest form, an arbitrary cross-section can
25	be defined by a series of points, segments and holes.
26	
27	.. figure:: ../_static/theory/arbitrary-section.png
28	  :width: 40%
29	  :alt: Arbitrary cross-sectio
30	  :align: center
31	
32	  Arbitrary cross-section with adopted axis convention.
33	
34	Mesh Generation
35	---------------
36	
37	The cross-section is meshed using quadratic superparametric triangular elements
38	(``Tri6``) using the `triangle library <https://github.com/drufat/triangle>`__ for
39	Python. Superparametric quadratic elements are defined as having straight edges and
40	mid-nodes located at the mid-point between adjacent corner nodes. ``triangle``
41	implements `Triangle <https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~quake/triangle.html>`__, which is a two
42	dimensional quality mesh generator and Delaunay triangulator written by Jonathan
43	Shewchuk in C.
44	
45	For the calculation of warping independent properties (i.e. area properties), the mesh
46	quality is not important as superparametric elements have a constant Jacobian and will
47	result in an exact solution independent of mesh quality. However, this is not the case
48	for the calculation of warping dependent properties. As a result, mesh quality and
49	refinement is critical and thus the user is encouraged to ensure an adequate mesh is
50	generated.
51	
52	Finite Element Preliminaries
53	----------------------------
54	
55	Element Type
56	~~~~~~~~~~~~
57	
58	Quadratic six noded triangular elements were implemented in ``sectionproperties`` in
59	order to utilise the finite element formulations for calculating section properties. The
60	figure below shows a generic six noded triangular element. As previously mentioned,
61	``sectionproperties`` implements superparametric elements, therefore the edges in the
62	below image will always be straight and not curved.
63	
64	.. figure:: ../_static/theory/six-noded-triangle.png
65	  :width: 40 %
66	  :alt: Six noded triangular element
67	  :align: center
68	
69	  Six noded triangular element [Felippa]_
70	
71	The quadratic triangular element was used due to the ease of mesh generation and
72	convergence advantages over the linear triangular element.
73	
74	Isoparametric Representation
75	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
76	
77	An isoparametric coordinate system has been used to evaluate the shape functions of the
78	parent element and map them to a generalised triangular element within the mesh. Three
79	independent isoparametric coordinates (:math:`\eta`, :math:`\xi`, :math:`\zeta`) are
80	used to map the six noded triangular element as shown in the figure below.
81	
82	.. figure:: ../_static/theory/isoparametric.png
83	  :width: 40 %
84	  :alt: Isoparametric coordinates for the two dimensional triangular element.
85	  :align: center
86	
87	  Isoparametric coordinates for the two dimensional triangular element.
88	
89	Shape Functions
90	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
91	
92	The shape functions for the six noded triangular element in terms of the isoparametric
93	coordinates are as follows:
94	
95	.. math::
96	  N_1 &= \eta (2 \eta - 1) \\
97	  N_2 &= \xi (2 \xi - 1) \\
98	  N_3 &= \zeta (2 \zeta - 1) \\
99	  N_4 &= 4 \eta \xi \\
100	  N_5 &= 4 \xi \zeta \\
101	  N_6 &= 4 \eta \zeta
102	
103	The above shape functions can be combined into the shape function row vector:
104	
105	.. math::
106	  \textbf{N} = [ N_1 \, N_2 \, N_3 \, N_4 \, N_5 \, N_6 ]
107	
108	Cartesian Partial Derivatives
109	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
110	
111	The partial derivatives of the shape functions with respect to the cartesian
112	coordinates, denoted as the :math:`\textbf{B}` matrix, are required in the finite
113	element formulations of various section properties. [Felippa]_ describes
114	the multiplication of the *Jacobian matrix* (:math:`\textbf{J}`) and the partial
115	derivative matrix (:math:`\textbf{P}`):
116	
117	.. math::
118	  \textbf{J P} =
119	  \begin{bmatrix}
120	    1 & 1 & 1 \\
121	    \sum x_i \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \eta} & \sum x_i \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \xi} & \sum x_i \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \zeta} \\
122	    \sum y_i \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \eta} & \sum y_i \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \xi} & \sum y_i \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \zeta} \\
123	  \end{bmatrix}
124	  \begin{bmatrix}
125	    \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial y} \\
126	    \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial y} \\
127	    \frac{\partial \zeta}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial \zeta}{\partial y} \\
128	  \end{bmatrix} =
129	  \begin{bmatrix}
130	    0 & 0 \\
131	    1 & 0 \\
132	    0 & 1 \\
133	  \end{bmatrix}
134	
135	The determinant of the *Jacobian matrix* scaled by one half is equal to the Jacobian:
136	
137	.. math::
138	  J = \frac{1}{2} \textrm{det} \, \textbf{J}
139	
140	The equation for :math:`\textbf{J P}` can be re-arranged to evaluate the partial
141	derivate matrix (:math:`\textbf{P}`):
142	
143	.. math::
144	  \textbf{P} = \textbf{J}^{-1}
145	  \begin{bmatrix}
146	  0 & 0 \\
147	  1 & 0 \\
148	  0 & 1 \\
149	  \end{bmatrix}
150	
151	As described in [Felippa]_, the derivates of the shape functions can be evaluated
152	using the below expressions:
153	
154	.. math::
155	  \textbf{B}^{\rm T}  =
156	  \begin{bmatrix}
157	    \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial y}
158	  \end{bmatrix} =
159	  \begin{bmatrix}
160	    \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \eta} & \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \xi} & \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial \zeta} \\
161	  \end{bmatrix}
162	  \begin{bmatrix}
163	    \textbf{P}
164	  \end{bmatrix}
165	
166	where the derivatives of the shape functions with respect to the isoparametric
167	parameters can easily be evaluated from the equation for the shape functions, resulting
168	in the following expression for the :math:`\textbf{B}` matrix:
169	
170	.. math::
171	  \textbf{B}^{\rm T}  =
172	  \begin{bmatrix}
173	    4 \eta - 1 & 0 & 0 \\
174	    0 & 4 \xi - 1 & 0 \\
175	    0 & 0 & 4 \zeta - 1 \\
176	    4 \xi & 4 \eta & 0 \\
177	    0 & 4 \zeta & 4 \xi \\
178	    4 \zeta & 0 & 4 \eta \\
179	  \end{bmatrix} \textbf{J}^{-1}
180	  \begin{bmatrix}
181	    0 & 0 \\
182	    1 & 0 \\
183	    0 & 1 \\
184	  \end{bmatrix}
185	
186	Numerical Integration
187	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
188	
189	Three different integration schemes are utilised in the cross-section analysis in order
190	to evaluate the integrals of varying order polynomials. The one point, three point and
191	six point integration schemes are summarised in the figure below [Felippa]_:
192	
193	.. list-table:: Six noded triangle integration schemes with maximum degree of polynomial
194	    that is evaluated exactly.
195	
196	   * - .. figure:: ../_static/theory/int1.png
197	          :width: 100 %
198	          :alt: 1pt integration; p-degree=1
199	          :align: center
200	
201	          1pt integration; p-degree=1
202	
203	     - .. figure:: ../_static/theory/int2.png
204	          :width: 100 %
205	          :alt: 3pt integration; p-degree=2
206	          :align: center
207	
208	          3pt integration; p-degree=2
209	
210	     - .. figure:: ../_static/theory/int3.png
211	          :width: 100 %
212	          :alt: 6pt integration; p-degree=4
213	          :align: center
214	
215	          6pt integration; p-degree=4
216	
217	The locations and weights of the Gauss points are summarised in the table below
218	[Felippa]_:
219	
220	+--------+-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
221	| Scheme | :math:`\eta`-location | :math:`\xi`-location | :math:`\zeta`-location | weight              |
222	+========+=======================+======================+========================+=====================+
223	| 1 pt.  | :math:`\frac{1}{3}`   | :math:`\frac{1}{3}`  | :math:`\frac{1}{3}`    | 1                   |
224	+--------+-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
225	|        | :math:`\frac{2}{3}`   | :math:`\frac{1}{6}`  | :math:`\frac{1}{6}`    | :math:`\frac{1}{3}` |
226	|        +-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
227	| 3 pt.  | :math:`\frac{1}{6}`   | :math:`\frac{2}{3}`  | :math:`\frac{1}{6}`    | :math:`\frac{1}{3}` |
228	|        +-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
229	|        | :math:`\frac{1}{6}`   | :math:`\frac{1}{6}`  | :math:`\frac{2}{3}`    | :math:`\frac{1}{3}` |
230	+--------+-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
231	|        | :math:`1 - 2 g_2`     | :math:`g_2`          | :math:`g_2`            | :math:`w_2`         |
232	|        +-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
233	|        | :math:`g_2`           | :math:`1 - 2 g_2`    | :math:`g_2`            | :math:`w_2`         |
234	|        +-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
235	|        | :math:`g_2`           | :math:`g_2`          | :math:`1 - 2 g_2`      | :math:`w_2`         |
236	| 6 pt.  +-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
237	|        | :math:`g_1`           | :math:`g_1`          | :math:`1 - 2 g_1`      | :math:`w_1`         |
238	|        +-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
239	|        | :math:`1 - 2 g_1`     | :math:`g_1`          | :math:`g_1`            | :math:`w_1`         |
240	|        +-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
241	|        | :math:`g_1`           | :math:`1 - 2 g_1`    | :math:`g_1`            | :math:`w_1`         |
242	+--------+-----------------------+----------------------+------------------------+---------------------+
243	
244	The parameters for the six point numerical integration are shown below:
245	
246	.. math::
247	  g_{1,2} &= \frac{1}{18} \left(8 - \sqrt{10} \pm \sqrt{38 - 44\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}}\right) \\
248	  w_{1,2} &= \frac{620 \pm \sqrt{213125-53320 \sqrt{10}}}{3720}
249	
250	Bringing together the isoparametric representation of the six noded triangular element
251	and numerical integration, the integration of a function :math:`f(\eta, \xi, \zeta)`
252	proves to be simpler than integrating the corresponding function :math:`f(x,y)` over the
253	cartesian element [Pilkey]_. The transformation formula for integrals is:
254	
255	.. math::
256	  \int_{\Omega} f(x,y) \, dx \, dy &= \int_{\Omega_r} f(\eta, \xi, \zeta) \, J \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
257	  &= \sum_i^n w_i f(\eta_i, \xi_i, \zeta_i) \, J_i
258	
259	where the sum is taken over the integration points, :math:`w_i` is the weight of the
260	current integration point and :math:`J_i` is the Jacobian at the current integration
261	point (recall that the Jacobian is constant for the superparametric six noded triangular
262	element).
263	
264	.. _label-extrapolation:
265	
266	Extrapolation to Nodes
267	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
268	
269	The most optimal location to sample stresses are at the integration points, however the
270	results are generally plotted using nodal values. As a result, the stresses at the
271	integration points need to be extrapolated to the nodes of the element. The extrapolated
272	stresses at the nodes (:math:`\tilde{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_g`) can be calculated through
273	the multiplication of a smoothing matrix (:math:`\textbf{H}`) and the stresses at the
274	integration points (:math:`\boldsymbol{\sigma}_g`) [Pilkey]_:
275	
276	.. math::
277	  \tilde{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_g = \textbf{H}^{-1} \, \boldsymbol{\sigma}_g
278	
279	where the :math:`\textbf{H}` matrix contains the row vectors of the shape functions at
280	each integration point:
281	
282	.. math::
283	  \textbf{H} =
284	  \begin{bmatrix}
285	    \textbf{N}(\eta_1, \xi_1, \zeta_1) \\
286	    \textbf{N}(\eta_2, \xi_2, \zeta_2) \\
287	    \textbf{N}(\eta_3, \xi_3, \zeta_3) \\
288	    \textbf{N}(\eta_4, \xi_4, \zeta_4) \\
289	    \textbf{N}(\eta_5, \xi_5, \zeta_5) \\
290	    \textbf{N}(\eta_6, \xi_6, \zeta_6) \\
291	  \end{bmatrix}
292	
293	Where two or more elements share the same node, nodal averaging is used to evaluate the
294	nodal stress.
295	
296	Lagrangian Multiplier
297	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
298	
299	As described in the calculation of the :ref:`label-theory-torsion` and
300	:ref:`label-theory-shear`, partial differential equations are to be solved
301	with purely Neumann boundary conditions. In the context of the torsion and shear
302	problem, this involves the inversion of a nearly singular global stiffness matrix. After
303	shifting the domain such that the centroid coincides with the global origin, the
304	Lagrangian multiplier method is used to solve the set of linear equations of the form
305	:math:`\textbf{K} \textbf{u} = \textbf{F}` by introducing an extra constraint on the
306	solution vector whereby the mean value is equal to zero. [Larson]_ et al.
307	describe the resulting modified stiffness matrix, and solution and load vector:
308	
309	.. math::
310	  \begin{bmatrix}
311	    \textbf{K} & \textbf{C}^{\rm{T}} \\
312	    \textbf{C} & 0 \\
313	  \end{bmatrix}
314	  \begin{bmatrix}
315	    \textbf{u} \\
316	    \lambda \\
317	  \end{bmatrix} =
318	  \begin{bmatrix}
319	    \textbf{F} \\
320	    0 \\
321	  \end{bmatrix}
322	
323	where :math:`\textbf{C}` is a row vector of ones and :math:`\lambda` may be though of as
324	a force acting to enforce the constraints, which should be relatively small when
325	compared to the values in the force vector and can be omitted from the solution vector.
326	
327	Calculation of Cross-Section Properties
328	---------------------------------------
329	
330	Cross-Sectional Area
331	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
332	
333	The area ``A`` of the cross-section is given by [Pilkey]_:
334	
335	.. math::
336	  A = \int_A dx \, dy = \sum_e A_e = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta
337	
338	As the Jacobian is constant over the element, the integration over the element domain in
339	the above equation can be performed using one point integration:
340	
341	.. math::
342	  A = \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^1 w_i J_i
343	
344	First Moments of Area
345	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
346	
347	The first moments of area are defined by [Pilkey]_:
348	
349	.. math::
350	  Q_x &= \int_A y \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \textbf{N} \textbf{y}_e J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
351	  Q_y &= \int_A x \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \textbf{N} \textbf{x}_e J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
352	
353	where :math:`\textbf{x}_e` and :math:`\textbf{y}_e` are column vectors containing the
354	cartesian coordinates of the element nodes. The above equations can be evaluated using
355	three point integration as the shape functions (:math:`\textbf{N}`) are quadratic:
356	
357	.. math::
358	  Q_x &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^3 w_i \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e J_e \\
359	  Q_y &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^3 w_i \textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e J_e \\
360	
361	Centroids
362	~~~~~~~~~
363	
364	The coordinates of the centroid are found from [Pilkey]_:
365	
366	.. math::
367	  x_c &= \frac{Q_y}{A} \\
368	  y_c &= \frac{Q_x}{A} \\
369	
370	Second Moments of Area
371	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
372	
373	The second moments of area are defined by [Pilkey]_:
374	
375	.. math::
376	  I_{xx} &= \int_A y^2 \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} (\textbf{N} \textbf{y}_e)^2 J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
377	  I_{yy} &= \int_A x^2 \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} (\textbf{N} \textbf{x}_e)^2 J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
378	  I_{xy} &= \int_A xy \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \textbf{N} \textbf{y}_e \textbf{N} \textbf{x}_e  J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
379	
380	The above equations can be evaluated using six point integration as the square of the
381	shape functions are quartic:
382	
383	.. math::
384	  I_{xx} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e)^2 J_e \\
385	  I_{yy} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e)^2 J_e \\
386	  I_{xy} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \textbf{N} \textbf{y}_e \textbf{N} \textbf{x}_e J_e \\
387	
388	The above equations list the second moments of area about the global coordinate system
389	axis, which is chosen arbitrarily by the user. These properties can be found about the
390	centroidal axis of the cross-section by using the parallel axis theorem:
391	
392	.. math::
393	  I_{\overline{xx}} &= I_{xx} - {y_c}^2 A = I_{xx} - \frac{{Q_x}^2}{A} \\
394	  I_{\overline{yy}} &= I_{yy} - {x_c}^2 A = I_{yy} - \frac{{Q_y}^2}{A} \\
395	  I_{\overline{xy}} &= I_{xy} - x_c y_c A = I_{xy} - \frac{Q_x Q_y}{A} \\
396	
397	Radii of Gyration
398	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
399	
400	The radii of gyration can be calculated from the second moments of area and the
401	cross-sectional area as follows [Pilkey]_:
402	
403	.. math::
404	  r_x = \sqrt{\frac{I_{xx}}{A}} \\
405	  r_y = \sqrt{\frac{I_{yy}}{A}} \\
406	
407	.. _label-theory-elastic-section-moduli:
408	
409	Elastic Section Moduli
410	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
411	
412	The elastic section modulii can be calculated from the second moments of area and the
413	extreme (min. and max.) coordinates of the cross-section in the x and y-directions
414	[Pilkey]_:
415	
416	.. math::
417	  Z_{xx}^+ = \frac{I_{\overline{xx}}}{y_{max} - y_c} \\
418	  Z_{xx}^- = \frac{I_{\overline{xx}}}{y_c - y_{min}} \\
419	  Z_{yy}^+ = \frac{I_{\overline{yy}}}{x_{max} - x_c} \\
420	  Z_{yy}^- = \frac{I_{\overline{yy}}}{x_c - x_{min}} \\
421	
422	.. _label-theory-plastic-section-moduli:
423	
424	Plastic Section Moduli
425	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
426	
427	For a homogenous section, the plastic centroid can be determined by finding the
428	intersection of the two lines that evenly divide the cross-sectional area in both the
429	:math:`x` and :math:`y` directions. A suitable procedure could not be found in
430	literature and thus an algorithm involving the iterative incrementation of the plastic
431	centroid was developed. The algorithm uses
432	`Brent's method <https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.brentq.html>`__
433	to efficiently locate the plastic centroidal axes in the global and principal
434	directions.
435	
436	Once the plastic centroid has been located, the plastic section moduli can be readily
437	computed using the following expression:
438	
439	.. math::
440	  S_{xx} &= \frac{A}{2} \left| y_{c,t} - y_{c,b} \right| \\
441	  S_{yy} &= \frac{A}{2} \left| x_{c,t} - x_{c,b} \right|
442	
443	where :math:`A` is the cross-sectional area, and :math:`x_{c,t}` and :math:`x_{c,b}`
444	refer to the centroids of the top half section and bottom half section respectively.
445	
446	Principal Axis Properties
447	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
448	
449	The principal bending axes are determined by calculating the principal moments of
450	inertia [Pilkey]_:
451	
452	.. math::
453	  I_{11} &= \frac{I_{\overline{xx}} + I_{\overline{yy}}}{2} + \Delta \\
454	  I_{22} &= \frac{I_{\overline{xx}} + I_{\overline{yy}}}{2} - \Delta \\
455	
456	where:
457	
458	.. math::
459	  \Delta = \sqrt{\left(\frac{I_{\overline{xx}} - I_{\overline{yy}}}{2}\right)^2 + {I_{\overline{xy}}}^2}
460	
461	The angle between the :math:`\bar{x}` axis and the axis belonging to the largest
462	principal moment of inertia can be computed as follows:
463	
464	.. math::
465	  \phi = {\tan}^{-1} \frac{I_{\overline{xx}} - I_{11}}{I_{\overline{xy}}}
466	
467	The prinicpal section moduli require the calculation of the perpendicular distance from
468	the principal axes to the extreme fibres. All the nodes in the mesh are considered with
469	vector algebra used to compute the perpendicular distances and the minimum and maximum
470	distances identified. The perpendicular distance from a point :math:`P` to a line
471	parallel to :math:`\overrightarrow{u}` that passes through :math:`Q` is given by:
472	
473	.. math::
474	  d = | \, \overrightarrow{PQ} \times \overrightarrow{u} \, |
475	
476	The location of the point is checked to see whether it is above or below the principal
477	axis. Again vector algebra is used to check this condition. The condition in the below
478	equation will result in the point being above the :math:`\overrightarrow{u}` axis.
479	
480	.. math::
481	  \overrightarrow{QP} \times \overrightarrow{u} < 0
482	
483	Using the above equations, the principal section moduli can be computed similar to that
484	in the calculation of the :ref:`label-theory-elastic-section-moduli` and
485	:ref:`label-theory-plastic-section-moduli`.
486	
487	.. _label-theory-torsion:
488	
489	Torsion Constant
490	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
491	
492	The Saint-Venant torsion constant (:math:`J`) can be obtained by solving the below
493	partial differential equation for the warping function, :math:`\omega`:
494	
495	.. math::
496	  \nabla^2 \omega = 0
497	
498	subject to the boundary condition described below:
499	
500	.. math::
501	  \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial x} n_x + \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial y} n_y = y n_x - x n_y
502	
503	[Pilkey]_ shows that by using the finite element method, this problem can be
504	reduced to a set of linear equations of the form:
505	
506	.. math::
507	  \textbf{K} \boldsymbol{\omega} = \textbf{F}
508	
509	where :math:`\textbf{K}` and :math:`\textbf{F}` are assembled through summation at
510	element level. The element equations for the :math:`e^{\textrm{th}}` element are:
511	
512	.. math::
513	  \textbf{k}^e \boldsymbol{\omega}^e = \textbf{f}^e
514	
515	with the stiffness matrix defined as:
516	
517	.. math::
518	  \textbf{k}^e = \int_{\Omega} \textbf{B}^{\rm T} \textbf{B} J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta
519	
520	and the load vector defined as:
521	
522	.. math::
523	  \textbf{f}^e = \int_{\Omega} \textbf{B}^{\rm T}
524	  \begin{bmatrix}
525	    \textbf{N} \textbf{y} \\
526	    -\textbf{N} \textbf{x} \\
527	  \end{bmatrix}
528	  J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta
529	
530	Applying numerical integration to the stiffness matrix and load vector results in the
531	following expressions:
532	
533	.. math::
534	  \textbf{k}^e &= \sum_{i=1}^3 w_i \textbf{B}_i^{\rm T} \textbf{B}_i J_e \\
535	  \textbf{f}^e &= \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \textbf{B}_i^{\rm T}
536	  \begin{bmatrix}
537	    \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e \\
538	    -\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e \\
539	  \end{bmatrix} J_e
540	
541	Once the warping function has been evaluated, the Saint-Venant torsion constant can be
542	calculated as follows:
543	
544	.. math::
545	  J = I_{xx} + I_{yy} - \boldsymbol{\omega}^{\rm T} \textbf{K} \boldsymbol{\omega}
546	
547	.. _label-theory-shear:
548	
549	Shear Properties
550	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
551	
552	The shear behaviour of the cross-section can be described by Saint-Venant's elasticity
553	solution for a homogenous prismatic beam subjected to transverse shear loads
554	[Pilkey]_. Through cross-section equilibrium and linear-elasticity, an expression
555	for the shear stresses resulting from a transverse shear load can be derived.
556	[Pilkey]_ explains that this is best done through the introduction of shear
557	functions, :math:`\Psi` and :math:`\Phi`, which describe the distribution of shear
558	stress within a cross-section resulting from an applied transverse load in the
559	:math:`x` and :math:`y` directions respectively. These shear functions can be obtained
560	by solving the following uncoupled partial differential equations:
561	
562	.. math::
563	  \nabla^2 \Psi &= 2(I_{\overline{xy}}  y - I_{\overline{xx}} x) \\
564	  \nabla^2 \Phi &= 2(I_{\overline{xy}} x - I_{\overline{yy}} y)
565	
566	subject to the respective boundary conditions:
567	
568	.. math::
569	  \frac{\partial \Psi}{\partial n} &= \textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{d} \\
570	  \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial n} &= \textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{h}
571	
572	where :math:`\textbf{n}` is the normal unit vector at the boundary and
573	:math:`\textbf{d}` and :math:`\textbf{h}` are defined as follows:
574	
575	.. math::
576	  \textbf{d} &= \nu \left(I_{\overline{xx}} \frac{x^2 -y^2}{2} - I_{\overline{xy}} xy\right) \textbf{i} + \nu \left(I_{\overline{xx}} xy + I_{\overline{xy}} \frac{x^2 -y^2}{2}\right) \textbf{j} \\
577	  \textbf{h} &= \nu \left(I_{\overline{yy}} xy - I_{\overline{xy}} \frac{x^2 -y^2}{2}\right) \textbf{i} - \nu \left(I_{\overline{xy}} xy + I_{\overline{yy}} \frac{x^2 -y^2}{2}\right) \textbf{j}
578	
579	[Pilkey]_ shows that the shear equations subject to the boundary conditions
580	can be solved using the finite element method. This results in a set of linear equations
581	at element level of the form:
582	
583	.. math::
584	  \textbf{k}^e \boldsymbol{\Psi}^e &= \textbf{f}^e_x \\
585	  \textbf{k}^e \boldsymbol{\Phi}^e &= \textbf{f}^e_y
586	
587	The local stiffness matrix, :math:`\textbf{k}^e`, is identical to the matrix used to
588	determine the torsion constant:
589	
590	.. math::
591	  \textbf{k}^e = \int_{\Omega} \textbf{B}^{\rm T} \textbf{B} J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta
592	
593	The load vectors are defined as:
594	
595	.. math::
596	  \textbf{f}^e_x &= \int_{\Omega} \left[\frac{\nu}{2} \textbf{B}^{\rm T}
597	  \begin{bmatrix}
598	    d_1 \\
599	    d_2\\
600	  \end{bmatrix}
601	  + 2 (1 + \nu) \textbf{N}^{\rm T} (I_{\overline{xx}} \textbf{N} \textbf{x} - I_{\overline{xy}} \textbf{N} \textbf{y}) \right] J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
602	  \textbf{f}^e_y &= \int_{\Omega} \left[\frac{\nu}{2} \textbf{B}^{\rm T}
603	  \begin{bmatrix}
604	    h_1 \\
605	    h_2\\
606	  \end{bmatrix}
607	  + 2 (1 + \nu) \textbf{N}^{\rm T} (I_{\overline{yy}} \textbf{N} \textbf{y} - I_{\overline{xy}} \textbf{N} \textbf{x}) \right] J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
608	
609	where:
610	
611	.. math::
612	  d_1 &= I_{\overline{xx}} r - I_{\overline{xy}} q & d_2 &= I_{\overline{xy}} r + I_{\overline{xx}} q \\
613	  h_1 &= -I_{\overline{xy}} r + I_{\overline{yy}} q & h_2 &= -I_{\overline{yy}} r - I_{\overline{xy}} q \\
614	  r &= (\textbf{N} \textbf{x})^2 - (\textbf{N} \textbf{y})^2 & q &= 2 \textbf{N} \textbf{x} \textbf{N} \textbf{y}
615	
616	Applying numerical integration to the stiffness matrix and load vector results in the
617	following expressions:
618	
619	.. math::
620	  \textbf{k}^e &= \sum_{i=1}^3 w_i \textbf{B}_i^{\rm T} \textbf{B}_i J_e \\
621	  \textbf{f}^e_x &= \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \left[\frac{\nu}{2} \textbf{B}_i^{\rm T}
622	  \begin{bmatrix}
623	    d_{1,i} \\
624	    d_{2,i} \\
625	  \end{bmatrix}
626	  + 2 (1 + \nu) \textbf{N}_i^{\rm T} (I_{\overline{xx}} \textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e - I_{\overline{xy}} \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e) \right] J_e \\
627	  \textbf{f}^e_y &= \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \left[\frac{\nu}{2} \textbf{B}_i^{\rm T}
628	  \begin{bmatrix}
629	    h_{1,i} \\
630	    h_{2,i} \\
631	  \end{bmatrix}
632	  + 2 (1 + \nu) \textbf{N}_i^{\rm T} (I_{\overline{yy}} \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e - I_{\overline{xy}} \textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e) \right] J_e \\
633	
634	Shear Centre
635	~~~~~~~~~~~~
636	
637	The shear centre can be computed consistently based on elasticity, or through Trefftz's
638	definition, which is based on thin-wall assumptions [Pilkey]_.
639	
640	**Elasticity:** [Pilkey]_ demonstrates that the coordinates of the shear
641	centre are given by the following expressions:
642	
643	.. math::
644	  x_s &= \frac{1}{\Delta_s} \left[ \frac{\nu}{2} \int_{\Omega} (I_{\overline{yy}} x + I_{\overline{xy}} y)\left(x^2+y^2 \right) \, d \Omega - \int_{\Omega} \textbf{g} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla \Phi} \, d \Omega\right] \\
645	  y_s &= \frac{1}{\Delta_s} \left[ \frac{\nu}{2} \int_{\Omega} (I_{\overline{xx}} y + I_{\overline{xy}} x)\left(x^2+y^2 \right) \, d \Omega + \int_{\Omega} \textbf{g} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla \Psi} \, d \Omega\right] \\
646	
647	where:
648	
649	.. math::
650	  \Delta_s &= 2 (1 + \nu)(I_{\overline{xx}} I_{\overline{yy}} - {I_{\overline{xy}}}^2) \\
651	  \textbf{g} &= y \textbf{i} - x \textbf{j}
652	
653	The first integral in shear centre equations can be evaluated using quadrature for each
654	element. The second integral can be simplified once the shear functions, :math:`\Psi`
655	and :math:`\Phi`, have been obtained:
656	
657	.. math::
658	  \int_{\Omega} \textbf{g} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla \Phi} \, d \Omega &= \textbf{F}^{\rm T} \boldsymbol{\Phi} \\
659	  \int_{\Omega} \textbf{g} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla \Psi} \, d \Omega &= \textbf{F}^{\rm T} \boldsymbol{\Psi}
660	
661	where :math:`\textbf{F}` is the global load vector determined for the torsion problem in
662	:ref:`label-theory-torsion`. The resulting expression for the shear centre therefore
663	becomes:
664	
665	.. math::
666	  x_s &= \frac{1}{\Delta_s} \Bigg[\Bigg(\frac{\nu}{2} \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i (I_{\overline{yy}} \textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e + I_{\overline{xy}} \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e)\Big((\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e)^2 + (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e)^2 \Big) J_e \Bigg) - \textbf{F}^{\rm T} \boldsymbol{\Phi} \Bigg] \\
667	  y_s &= \frac{1}{\Delta_s} \Bigg[ \Bigg(\frac{\nu}{2} \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i (I_{\overline{xx}} \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e + I_{\overline{xy}} \textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e)\Big((\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e)^2 + (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e)^2 \Big) J_e \Bigg) + \textbf{F}^{\rm T} \boldsymbol{\Psi} \Bigg]
668	
669	**Trefftz's Definition:** Using thin walled assumptions, the shear centre coordinates
670	according to Trefftz's definition are given by:
671	
672	.. math::
673	  x_s &= \frac{I_{\overline{xy}} I_{x \omega} - I_{\overline{yy}} I_{y \omega}}{I_{\overline{xx}} I_{\overline{yy}}  - {I_{\overline{xy}}}^2} \\
674	  y_s &= \frac{I_{\overline{xx}} I_{x \omega} - I_{\overline{xy}} I_{y \omega}}{I_{\overline{xx}} I_{\overline{yy}}  - {I_{\overline{xy}}}^2}
675	
676	where the sectorial products of area are defined as:
677	
678	.. math::
679	  I_{x\omega} &= \int_{\Omega} x \omega(x,y) \, d \Omega \\
680	  I_{y\omega} &= \int_{\Omega} y \omega(x,y) \, d \Omega
681	
682	The finite element implementation of the above integrals are shown below:
683	
684	.. math::
685	  I_{x\omega} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e \textbf{N}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_e J_e \\
686	  I_{y\omega} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e \textbf{N}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_e J_e \\
687	
688	Shear Deformation Coefficients
689	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
690	
691	The shear deformation coefficients are used to calculate the shear area of the section
692	as a result of transverse loading. The shear area is defined as :math:`A_s = k_s A`.
693	[Pilkey]_ describes the finite element formulation used to determine the
694	shear deformation coefficients:
695	
696	.. math::
697	  \kappa_x &= \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \left(\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{e\rm{T}} \textbf{B}^{\rm{T}} - \textbf{d}^{\rm{T}}\right) \left(\textbf{B} \boldsymbol{\Psi}^e - \textbf{d}\right) J_e \, d\Omega \\
698	  \kappa_y &= \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \left(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{e\rm{T}} \textbf{B}^{\rm{T}} - \textbf{h}^{\rm{T}}\right) \left(\textbf{B} \boldsymbol{\Phi}^e - \textbf{h}\right) J_e \, d\Omega \\
699	  \kappa_{xy} &= \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \left(\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{e\rm{T}} \textbf{B}^{\rm{T}} - \textbf{d}^{\rm{T}}\right) \left(\textbf{B} \boldsymbol{\Phi}^e - \textbf{h}\right) J_e \, d\Omega \\
700	
701	where the shear areas are related to :math:`\kappa_x` and :math:`\kappa_y` by:
702	
703	.. math::
704	  k_{s,x} A &= \frac{{\Delta_s}^2}{\kappa_x} \\
705	  k_{s,y} A &= \frac{{\Delta_s}^2}{\kappa_y} \\
706	  k_{s,xy} A &= \frac{{\Delta_s}^2}{\kappa_{xy}} \\
707	
708	The finite element formulation of the shear deformation coefficients is described below:
709	
710	.. math::
711	  \kappa_x &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \left(\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{e\rm{T}} \textbf{B}_i^{\rm{T}} - \frac{\nu}{2}
712	  \begin{bmatrix}
713	    d_{1,i} \\
714	    d_{2,i} \\
715	  \end{bmatrix}^{\rm{T}}\right) \left(\textbf{B}_i \boldsymbol{\Psi}^e - \frac{\nu}{2}
716	  \begin{bmatrix}
717	    d_{1,i} \\
718	    d_{2,i} \\
719	  \end{bmatrix}\right) J_e \\
720	  \kappa_y &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \left(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{e\rm{T}} \textbf{B}_i^{\rm{T}} - \frac{\nu}{2}
721	  \begin{bmatrix}
722	    h_{1,i} \\
723	    h_{2,i} \\
724	  \end{bmatrix}^{\rm{T}}\right) \left(\textbf{B}_i \boldsymbol{\Phi}^e - \frac{\nu}{2}
725	  \begin{bmatrix}
726	    h_{1,i} \\
727	    h_{2,i} \\
728	  \end{bmatrix}\right) J_e \\
729	  \kappa_{xy} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \left(\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{e\rm{T}} \textbf{B}_i^{\rm{T}} - \frac{\nu}{2}
730	  \begin{bmatrix}
731	    d_{1,i} \\
732	    d_{2,i} \\
733	  \end{bmatrix}^{\rm{T}}\right) \left(\textbf{B}_i \boldsymbol{\Phi}^e - \frac{\nu}{2}
734	  \begin{bmatrix}
735	    h_{1,i} \\
736	    h_{2,i} \\
737	  \end{bmatrix}\right) J_e \\
738	
739	Warping Constant
740	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
741	
742	The warping constant, :math:`\Gamma`, can be calculated from the warping function
743	(:math:`\omega`) and the coordinates of the shear centre [Pilkey]_:
744	
745	.. math::
746	  \Gamma = I_{\omega} - \frac{{Q_{\omega}}^2}{A} - y_s I_{x\omega} + x_s I_{y\omega}
747	
748	where the warping moments are calculated as follows:
749	
750	.. math::
751	  Q_{\omega} &= \int_{\Omega} \omega \, d\Omega = \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^3 w_i \textbf{N}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_e J_e \\
752	  I_{\omega} &= \int_{\Omega} \omega^2 \, d\Omega = \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i (\textbf{N}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_e)^2 J_e
753	
754	Monosymmetry Constants
755	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
756	
757	The monosymmetry constants are used to evaluate buckling in sections with unequal
758	flanges. The constants are calculated in accordance with the formula provided in
759	AS 4100-1998 [AS4100]_:
760	
761	.. math::
762	  \beta_x &= \frac{1}{I_{xx}} \int_{\Omega} x^2 y + y^3 d\Omega - 2y_s \\
763	  \beta_y &= \frac{1}{I_{yy}} \int_{\Omega} x y^2 + x^3 d\Omega - 2x_s \\
764	
765	The finite element formulation of the above integrals is described below:
766	
767	.. math::
768	  \int_{\Omega} x^2 y + y^3 d\Omega &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \left[(\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e)^2 \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e + (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e)^3 \right] J_e \\
769	  \int_{\Omega} x y^2 + x^3 d\Omega &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \left[\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e)^2 + (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e)^3 \right] J_e \\
770	
771	Cross-Section Stresses
772	----------------------
773	
774	Cross-section stresses resulting from an axial force, bending moments, a torsion moment
775	and shear forces, can be evaluated at the integration points within each element.
776	:ref:`label-extrapolation` describes the process of extrapolating the stresses to the
777	element nodes and the combination of the results with the adjacent elements through
778	nodal averaging.
779	
780	Axial Stresses
781	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
782	
783	The normal stress resulting from an axial force :math:`N_{zz}` at any point :math:`i` is
784	given by:
785	
786	.. math::
787	  \sigma_{zz} = \frac{N_{zz}}{A}
788	
789	Bending Stresses
790	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
791	
792	Global Axis Bending
793	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
794	
795	The normal stress resulting from a bending moments :math:`M_{xx}` and :math:`M_{yy}` at
796	any point :math:`i` is given by [Pilkey]_:
797	
798	.. math::
799	  \sigma_{zz} = -\frac{I_{\overline{xy}} M_{xx} + I_{\overline{xx}} M_{yy}}{I_{\overline{xx}} I_{\overline{yy}} - {I_{\overline{xy}}}^2} \overline{x}_i + \frac{I_{\overline{yy}} M_{xx} + I_{\overline{xy}} M_{yy}}{I_{\overline{xx}} I_{\overline{yy}} - {I_{\overline{xy}}}^2} \overline{y}_i
800	
801	Principal Axis Bending
802	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
803	
804	Similarly, the normal stress resulting from a bending moments :math:`M_{11}` and
805	:math:`M_{22}` at any point :math:`i` is given by:
806	
807	.. math::
808	  \sigma_{zz} = -\frac{M_{22}}{I_{\overline{22}}} \overline{x}_{1,i} + \frac{M_{11}}{I_{\overline{11}}} \overline{y}_{2,i}
809	
810	Torsion Stresses
811	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
812	
813	The shear stresses resulting from a torsion moment :math:`M_{zz}` at any point :math:`i`
814	within an element :math:`e` are given by [Pilkey]_:
815	
816	.. math::
817	  \boldsymbol{\tau}^e =
818	  \begin{bmatrix}
819	    \tau_{zx} \\
820	    \tau_{zy} \\
821	  \end{bmatrix}^e = \frac{M_{zz}}{J} \left(\textbf{B}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}^e -
822	  \begin{bmatrix}
823	    \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e \\
824	    -\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e \\
825	  \end{bmatrix}\right)
826	
827	Shear Stresses
828	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
829	
830	The shear stresses resulting from transverse shear forces :math:`V_{xx}` and
831	:math:`V_{yy}` at any point :math:`i` within an element :math:`e` are given by
832	[Pilkey]_:
833	
834	.. math::
835	  \begin{bmatrix}
836	    \tau_{zx} \\
837	    \tau_{zy} \\
838	  \end{bmatrix}^e = \frac{V_{xx}}{\Delta_s} \left(\textbf{B}_i \boldsymbol{\Psi}^e - \frac{\nu}{2}
839	  \begin{bmatrix}
840	    d_{1,i} \\
841	    d_{2,i} \\
842	  \end{bmatrix}\right) + \frac{V_{yy}}{\Delta_s} \left(\textbf{B}_i \boldsymbol{\Phi}^e - \frac{\nu}{2}
843	  \begin{bmatrix}
844	    h_{1,i} \\
845	    h_{2,i} \\
846	  \end{bmatrix}\right)
847	
848	von Mises Stresses
849	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
850	
851	The von Mises stress can be determined from the net axial and shear stress as follows
852	[Pilkey]_:
853	
854	.. math::
855	  \sigma_{vM} = \sqrt{{\sigma_{zz}}^2 + 3({\tau_{zx}}^2 + {\tau_{zy}}^2)}
856	
857	Principal Stresses
858	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
859	
860	For a cross section subjected to axial force, shear in the :math:`x` and :math:`y` axes
861	which are perpendicular to the centroidal (:math:`z`) axis, and moments about all three
862	axes, there are no axial stresses in the :math:`x` or :math:`y` axes, and so the stress
863	tensor is given by:
864	
865	.. math::
866	    \boldsymbol{\sigma} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \tau_{zx} \\
867	                               0 & 0 & \tau_{zy} \\
868	                           \tau_{xz} & \tau_{yz} & \sigma_{zz}
869	                       \end{bmatrix}
870	
871	and of course the complementary shear stresses are equal, :math:`\tau_{zx}=\tau_{xz}`,
872	:math:`\tau_{zy}=\tau_{yz}`.
873	
874	By definition, the principal stresses are those for which the stress tensor becomes a
875	diagonal matrix through a coordinate transformation. Since this is the basic eigenvalue
876	problem, the principal stresses are then given by:
877	
878	.. math::
879	    \det (\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \lambda \textbf{I}) = 0
880	
881	Of which the characteristic polynomial can then be written:
882	
883	.. math::
884	    \lambda^3 - I_1\lambda^2 + I_2\lambda - I_3 = 0
885	
886	where the stress invariants :math:`I` are then given by [Onate]_:
887	
888	.. math::
889	    I_1 &= \textrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \sigma_{zz} \\
890	    I_2 &= \frac{1}{2}\left[\textrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})^2 - \textrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2) \right] = -\tau_{zx}^2 - \tau_{zy}^2 \\
891	    I_3 &= \det(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = 0
892	
893	and thus, the cubic polynomial reduces to a quadratic, the two roots of which are then
894	the first and third principal stresses (with :math:`\sigma_2 = 0`):
895	
896	.. math::
897	    \sigma_{1,3} = \frac{\sigma_{zz}}{2} \pm \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\sigma_{zz}}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{zx}^2 + \tau_{zy}^2  }
898	
899	.. _label-theory-composite:
900	
901	Composite Cross-Sections
902	------------------------
903	
904	[Pilkey]_ explains that composite cross-sections can be analysed using a
905	modulus-weighted approach in which the differential area element is multiplied by the
906	elastic modulus for the element, :math:`E_e`:
907	
908	.. math::
909	  d \widetilde{A} = E_e \, dA
910	
911	The expression for section properties after the application of numerical integration
912	then becomes:
913	
914	.. math::
915	  \int f(x,y) \, d \widetilde{A} = \sum_i^n w_i f(\eta_i, \xi_i, \zeta_i) \, J_i E_e
916	
917	[Pilkey]_ also notes that an assumption of the elastic cross-sectional
918	analysis of warping and shear is that:
919	
920	.. math::
921	  \sigma_x = \sigma_y = \tau_{xy} = 0
922	
923	However, for composite sections with variable Poisson's ratios, this assumption does not
924	hold. [Pilkey]_ does mention that engineering materials often have very
925	similar Poisson's ratios and therefore the difference can be negligible.
926	
927	.. note::
928	  If the Poisson's ratio of two materials used in a composite analysis are vastly
929	  different, the assumptions used in ``sectionproperties`` may not hold, see Chapter 5 &
930	  6 of [Pilkey]_.
931	
932	For the warping and shear analysis of composite cross-sections, ``sectionproperties``
933	defines an area based on an effective Poisson's ratio that is used to calculate the
934	relevant properties described above:
935	
936	.. math::
937	  \nu_{eff} = \frac{(E.A)_g}{2 (G.A)_g} - 1
938	
939	References
940	----------
941	
942	.. [Felippa] C. A. Felippa, *Introduction to Finite Element Methods*, Department of
943	    Aerospace Engineering Sciences and Center for Aerospace Structures University of
944	    Colorado, Boulder, Colorado, 2004.
945	
946	.. [Pilkey] W. D. Pilkey, *Analysis and Design of Elastic Beams: Computational Methods*,
947	    John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York, 2002.
948	
949	.. [Larson] M. G. Larson, F. Bengzon, *The Finite Element Method: Theory,
950	    Implementation, and Applications*, Vol. 10, Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg, 2013.
951	    doi:10.1007/978-3-642-33287-6.
952	
953	.. [AS4100] Standards Australia, *AS 4100 - 1998: Steel Structures (1998)*.
954	
955	.. [Onate] Oñate, E. (2009), *Structural Analysis with the Finite Element Method. Linear
956	    Statics. Volume 1: The Basis and Solids*, Springer Netherlands
957

events.text:
The theory defines first moments of area as unweighted: Qx = ∫ y dA, Qy = ∫ x dA. For composite sections, the modulus-weighted approach is used for the section properties, i.e. dÃ = E_e dA. So `qx` and `qy` become modulus-weighted: Qx = ∫ E y dA.

The package's `get_q()` returns these modulus-weighted moments for composite sections. This is the bug per the task: "the package's ordinary first-moment result is finite but incompatible with that construction observation, without clearly reporting that the requested result is unavailable."

474	            ixx: Second moment of area about the centroidal x-axis
475	            iyy: Second moment of area about the centroidal y-axis
476	            ixy: Second moment of area about the centroidal xy-axis
477	            i11: Second moment of area about the principal 11-axis
478	            i22: Second moment of area about the principal 22-axis
479	            phi: Principal bending axis angle
480	            j: St. Venant torsion constant
481	            nu: Effective Poisson's ratio for the cross-section
482	            omega: Values of the warping function at the element nodes
483	            psi_shear: Values of the psi shear function at the element nodes
484	            phi_shear: Values of the phi shear function at the element nodes
485	            delta_s: Cross-section shear factor
486	
487	        Returns:
488	            Tuple containing element stresses and integration weights
489	            (:math:`\sigma_{zz,n}`, :math:`\sigma_{zz,mxx}`,
490	            :math:`\sigma_{zz,myy}`, :math:`\sigma_{zz,m11}`,
491	            :math:`\sigma_{zz,m22}`, :math:`\sigma_{zx,mzz}`,
492	            :math:`\sigma_{zy,mzz}`, :math:`\sigma_{zx,vx}`,
493	            :math:`\sigma_{zy,vx}`, :math:`\sigma_{zx,vy}`,
494	            :math:`\sigma_{zy,vy}`, :math:`w_i`)
495	        """
496	        # calculate axial stress
497	        sig_zz_n = n * np.ones(6) * self.material.elastic_modulus / ea
498	
499	        # initialise stresses at the gauss points
500	        sig_zz_mxx_gp = np.zeros((6, 1))
501	        sig_zz_myy_gp = np.zeros((6, 1))
502	        sig_zz_m11_gp = np.zeros((6, 1))
503	        sig_zz_m22_gp = np.zeros((6, 1))
504	        sig_zxy_mzz_gp = np.zeros((6, 2))
505	        sig_zxy_vx_gp = np.zeros((6, 2))
506	        sig_zxy_vy_gp = np.zeros((6, 2))
507	
508	        # Gauss points for 6 point Gaussian integration
509	        gps = gauss_points(n=6)
510	
511	        for i, gp in enumerate(gps):
512	            # determine x and y positions with respect to the centroidal axis
513	            coords_c = np.zeros((2, 6))
514	            coords_c[0, :] = self.coords[0, :] - cx
515	            coords_c[1, :] = self.coords[1, :] - cy
516	
517	            # determine shape function, shape function derivative and jacobian
518	            n_shape, b, _ = shape_function(coords=coords_c, gauss_point=gp)
519	
520	            # determine x and y position at Gauss point
521	            nx = np.dot(n_shape, np.transpose(coords_c[0, :]))
522	            ny = np.dot(n_shape, np.transpose(coords_c[1, :]))
523	
524	            # determine 11 and 22 position at Gauss point
525	            nx_11, ny_22 = principal_coordinate(phi=phi, x=nx, y=ny)
526	
527	            # determine shear parameters
528	            r = nx**2 - ny**2
529	            q = 2 * nx * ny
530	            d1 = ixx * r - ixy * q
531	            d2 = ixy * r + ixx * q
532	            h1 = -ixy * r + iyy * q
533	            h2 = -iyy * r - ixy * q
534	
535	            # calculate element stresses
536	            sig_zz_mxx_gp[i, :] = self.material.elastic_modulus * (
537	                -(ixy * mxx) / (ixx * iyy - ixy**2) * nx
538	                + (iyy * mxx) / (ixx * iyy - ixy**2) * ny
539	            )
540	            sig_zz_myy_gp[i, :] = self.material.elastic_modulus * (
541	                -(ixx * myy) / (ixx * iyy - ixy**2) * nx
542	                + (ixy * myy) / (ixx * iyy - ixy**2) * ny
543	            )
544	            sig_zz_m11_gp[i, :] = self.material.elastic_modulus * m11 / i11 * ny_22
545	            sig_zz_m22_gp[i, :] = self.material.elastic_modulus * -m22 / i22 * nx_11
546	
547	            if mzz != 0:
548	                sig_zxy_mzz_gp[i, :] = (
549	                    self.material.elastic_modulus
550	                    * mzz
551	                    / j
552	                    * (b.dot(omega) - np.array([ny, -nx]))
553	                )
554	
555	            if vx != 0:
556	                sig_zxy_vx_gp[i, :] = (
557	                    self.material.elastic_modulus
558	                    * vx
559	                    / delta_s
560	                    * (b.dot(psi_shear) - nu / 2 * np.array([d1, d2]))
561	                )
562	
563	            if vy != 0:
564	                sig_zxy_vy_gp[i, :] = (
565	                    self.material.elastic_modulus
566	                    * vy
567	                    / delta_s
568	                    * (b.dot(phi_shear) - nu / 2 * np.array([h1, h2]))
569	                )
570	
571	        # extrapolate results to nodes
572	        sig_zz_mxx = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zz_mxx_gp[:, 0])
573	        sig_zz_myy = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zz_myy_gp[:, 0])
574	        sig_zz_m11 = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zz_m11_gp[:, 0])
575	        sig_zz_m22 = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zz_m22_gp[:, 0])
576	        sig_zx_mzz = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zxy_mzz_gp[:, 0])
577	        sig_zy_mzz = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zxy_mzz_gp[:, 1])
578	        sig_zx_vx = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zxy_vx_gp[:, 0])
579	        sig_zy_vx = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zxy_vx_gp[:, 1])
580	        sig_zx_vy = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zxy_vy_gp[:, 0])
581	        sig_zy_vy = extrapolate_to_nodes(w=sig_zxy_vy_gp[:, 1])
582	
583	        return (
584	            sig_zz_n,
585	            sig_zz_mxx,
586	            sig_zz_myy,
587	            sig_zz_m11,
588	            sig_zz_m22,
589	            sig_zx_mzz,
590	            sig_zy_mzz,
591	            sig_zx_vx,
592	            sig_zy_vx,
593	            sig_zx_vy,
594	            sig_zy_vy,
595	            gps[:, 0],
596	        )

598	    def local_element_stress(
599	        self,
600	        p: tuple[float, float],
601	        n: float,
602	        mxx: float,
603	        myy: float,
604	        m11: float,
605	        m22: float,
606	        mzz: float,
607	        vx: float,
608	        vy: float,
609	        ea: float,
610	        cx: float,
611	        cy: float,
612	        ixx: float,
613	        iyy: float,
614	        ixy: float,
615	        i11: float,
616	        i22: float,
617	        phi: float,
618	        j: float,
619	        nu: float,
620	        omega: np.ndarray,
621	        psi_shear: np.ndarray,
622	        phi_shear: np.ndarray,
623	        delta_s: float,
624	    ) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
625	        r"""Calculates the stress at a point resulting from a specified loading.
626	
627	        Args:
628	            p: Point (``x``, ``y``) in the global coordinate system that is within the
629	                element
630	            n: Axial force
631	            mxx: Bending moment about the centroidal xx-axis
632	            myy: Bending moment about the centroidal yy-axis
633	            m11: Bending moment about the centroidal 11-axis
634	            m22: Bending moment about the centroidal 22-axis
635	            mzz: Torsion moment about the centroidal zz-axis
636	            vx: Shear force acting in the x-direction
637	            vy: Shear force acting in the y-direction
638	            ea: Modulus weighted area
639	            cx: x position of the elastic centroid
640	            cy: y position of the elastic centroid
641	            ixx: Second moment of area about the centroidal x-axis
642	            iyy: Second moment of area about the centroidal y-axis
643	            ixy: Second moment of area about the centroidal xy-axis
644	            i11: Second moment of area about the principal 11-axis
645	            i22: Second moment of area about the principal 22-axis
646	            phi: Principal bending axis angle
647	            j: St. Venant torsion constant
648	            nu: Effective Poisson's ratio for the cross-section
649	            omega: Values of the warping function at the element nodes
650	            psi_shear: Values of the psi shear function at the element nodes
651	            phi_shear: Values of the phi shear function at the element nodes
652	            delta_s: Cross-section shear factor
653	
654	        Returns:
655	            Tuple containing stress values at point ``p`` (:math:`\sigma_{zz}`,
656	            :math:`\sigma_{zx}`, :math:`\sigma_{zy}`)
657	        """
658	        # get the elements nodal stress
659	        (
660	            sig_zz_n_el,
661	            sig_zz_mxx_el,
662	            sig_zz_myy_el,
663	            sig_zz_m11_el,
664	            sig_zz_m22_el,
665	            sig_zx_mzz_el,
666	            sig_zy_mzz_el,
667	            sig_zx_vx_el,
668	            sig_zy_vx_el,
669	            sig_zx_vy_el,
670	            sig_zy_vy_el,
671	            _,
672	        ) = self.element_stress(
673	            n=n,
674	            mxx=mxx,
675	            myy=myy,
676	            m11=m11,
677	            m22=m22,
678	            mzz=mzz,
679	            vx=vx,
680	            vy=vy,
681	            ea=ea,
682	            cx=cx,
683	            cy=cy,
684	            ixx=ixx,
685	            iyy=iyy,
686	            ixy=ixy,
687	            i11=i11,
688	            i22=i22,
689	            phi=phi,
690	            j=j,
691	            nu=nu,
692	            omega=omega,
693	            psi_shear=psi_shear,
694	            phi_shear=phi_shear,
695	            delta_s=delta_s,
696	        )
697	
698	        # get the local coordinates of the point within the reference element
699	        p_local = self.local_coord(p=p)
700	
701	        # get the value of the basis functions at p_local
702	        n_shape = shape_function_only(p=p_local)
703	
704	        # interpolate the nodal values to p_local and add the results
705	        (
706	            sig_zz_n_p,
707	            sig_zz_mxx_p,
708	            sig_zz_myy_p,
709	            sig_zz_m11_p,
710	            sig_zz_m22_p,
711	            sig_zx_mzz_p,
712	            sig_zy_mzz_p,
713	            sig_zx_vx_p,
714	            sig_zy_vx_p,
715	            sig_zx_vy_p,
716	            sig_zy_vy_p,
717	        ) = np.dot(
718	            np.array(
719	                [
720	                    sig_zz_n_el,
721	                    sig_zz_mxx_el,
722	                    sig_zz_myy_el,
723	                    sig_zz_m11_el,
724	                    sig_zz_m22_el,
725	                    sig_zx_mzz_el,
726	                    sig_zy_mzz_el,
727	                    sig_zx_vx_el,
728	                    sig_zy_vx_el,
729	                    sig_zx_vy_el,
730	                    sig_zy_vy_el,
731	                ]
732	            ),
733	            n_shape,
734	        )
735	        sig_zz_m_p = sig_zz_mxx_p + sig_zz_myy_p + sig_zz_m11_p + sig_zz_m22_p
736	        sig_zx_v_p = sig_zx_vx_p + sig_zx_vy_p
737	        sig_zy_v_p = sig_zy_vx_p + sig_zy_vy_p
738	        sig_zz_p = sig_zz_n_p + sig_zz_m_p
739	        sig_zx_p = sig_zx_mzz_p + sig_zx_v_p
740	        sig_zy_p = sig_zy_mzz_p + sig_zy_v_p
741	
742	        return (
743	            sig_zz_p,
744	            sig_zx_p,
745	            sig_zy_p,
746	        )

748	    def point_within_element(
749	        self,
750	        pt: tuple[float, float],
751	    ) -> bool:
752	        """Determines whether a point lies within the current element.
753	
754	        Args:
755	            pt: Point to check (``x``, ``y``)
756	
757	        Returns:
758	            Whether the point lies within an element
759	        """
760	        px = pt[0]
761	        py = pt[1]
762	
763	        # get coordinates of corner points
764	        x1: float = self.coords[0][0]
765	        y1: float = self.coords[1][0]
766	        x2: float = self.coords[0][1]
767	        y2: float = self.coords[1][1]
768	        x3: float = self.coords[0][2]
769	        y3: float = self.coords[1][2]
770	
771	        # compute variables alpha, beta and gamma
772	        alpha = ((y2 - y3) * (px - x3) + (x3 - x2) * (py - y3)) / (
773	            (y2 - y3) * (x1 - x3) + (x3 - x2) * (y1 - y3)
774	        )
775	        beta = ((y3 - y1) * (px - x3) + (x1 - x3) * (py - y3)) / (
776	            (y2 - y3) * (x1 - x3) + (x3 - x2) * (y1 - y3)
777	        )
778	        gamma = 1.0 - alpha - beta
779	
780	        # if the point lies within an element
781	        if alpha >= 0 and beta >= 0 and gamma >= 0:
782	            return True
783	        else:
784	            return False

786	    def local_coord(
787	        self,
788	        p: tuple[float, float],
789	    ) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
790	        """Maps a global point onto a local point.
791	
792	        Args:
793	            p: Global coordinate (``x``, ``y``)
794	
795	        Returns:
796	            Point in local coordinates (``eta``, ``xi``, ``zeta``)
797	        """
798	        eta, xi = np.dot(self._m, p - self._x0)
799	        zeta = 1 - eta - xi
800	        return eta, xi, zeta

803	def gauss_points(n: int) -> np.ndarray:
804	    """Gaussian weights and locations for ``n`` point Gaussian integration of a Tri6.
805	
806	    Args:
807	        n: Number of Gauss points (1, 3 or 6)
808	
809	    Raises:
810	        ValueError: ``n`` is invalid
811	
812	    Returns:
813	        An ``n x 4`` matrix consisting of the integration weight and the ``eta``, ``xi``
814	        and ``zeta`` locations for ``n`` Gauss points
815	    """
816	    if n == 1:
817	        # one point gaussian integration
818	        return np.array([[1.0, 1.0 / 3, 1.0 / 3, 1.0 / 3]], dtype=float)
819	
820	    elif n == 3:
821	        # three point gaussian integration
822	        return np.array(
823	            [
824	                [1.0 / 3, 2.0 / 3, 1.0 / 6, 1.0 / 6],
825	                [1.0 / 3, 1.0 / 6, 2.0 / 3, 1.0 / 6],
826	                [1.0 / 3, 1.0 / 6, 1.0 / 6, 2.0 / 3],
827	            ],
828	            dtype=float,
829	        )
830	    elif n == 6:
831	        # six point gaussian integration
832	        g1 = 1.0 / 18 * (8 - np.sqrt(10) + np.sqrt(38 - 44 * np.sqrt(2.0 / 5)))
833	        g2 = 1.0 / 18 * (8 - np.sqrt(10) - np.sqrt(38 - 44 * np.sqrt(2.0 / 5)))
834	        w1 = (620 + np.sqrt(213125 - 53320 * np.sqrt(10))) / 3720
835	        w2 = (620 - np.sqrt(213125 - 53320 * np.sqrt(10))) / 3720
836	
837	        return np.array(
838	            [
839	                [w2, 1 - 2 * g2, g2, g2],
840	                [w2, g2, 1 - 2 * g2, g2],
841	                [w2, g2, g2, 1 - 2 * g2],
842	                [w1, g1, g1, 1 - 2 * g1],
843	                [w1, 1 - 2 * g1, g1, g1],
844	                [w1, g1, 1 - 2 * g1, g1],
845	            ],
846	            dtype=float,
847	        )
848	    else:
849	        raise ValueError("n must be 1, 3 or 6.")

852	def shape_function(
853	    coords: np.ndarray,
854	    gauss_point: tuple[float, float, float, float],
855	) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, float]:
856	    """Calculates shape functions, derivates and the Jacobian determinant.
857	
858	    Computes the shape functions, shape function derivatives and the determinant of the
859	    Jacobian matrix for a ``Tri6`` element at a given Gauss point.
860	
861	    Args:
862	        coords: Global coordinates of the quadratic triangle vertices, of size
863	            ``[2 x 6]``
864	        gauss_point: Gaussian weight and isoparametric location of the Gauss point
865	
866	    Returns:
867	        The value of the shape functions ``N(i)`` at the given Gauss point
868	        (``[1 x 6]``), the derivative of the shape functions in the *j-th* global
869	        direction ``B(i,j)`` (``[2 x 6]``) and the determinant of the Jacobian
870	        matrix ``j``
871	    """
872	    # location of isoparametric co-ordinates for each Gauss point
873	    eta = gauss_point[1]
874	    xi = gauss_point[2]
875	    zeta = gauss_point[3]
876	
877	    # value of the shape functions
878	    n = np.array(
879	        [
880	            eta * (2 * eta - 1),
881	            xi * (2 * xi - 1),
882	            zeta * (2 * zeta - 1),
883	            4 * eta * xi,
884	            4 * xi * zeta,
885	            4 * eta * zeta,
886	        ],
887	        dtype=float,
888	    )
889	
890	    # derivatives of the shape functions wrt the isoparametric co-ordinates
891	    b_iso = np.array(
892	        [
893	            [4 * eta - 1, 0, 0, 4 * xi, 0, 4 * zeta],
894	            [0, 4 * xi - 1, 0, 4 * eta, 4 * zeta, 0],
895	            [0, 0, 4 * zeta - 1, 0, 4 * xi, 4 * eta],
896	        ],
897	        dtype=float,
898	    )
899	
900	    # form Jacobian matrix
901	    j_upper = np.array([[1, 1, 1]])
902	    j_lower = np.dot(coords, np.transpose(b_iso))
903	    j = np.vstack((j_upper, j_lower))
904	
905	    # calculate the jacobian
906	    jacobian = 0.5 * np.linalg.det(j)
907	
908	    # if the area of the element is not zero
909	    if jacobian != 0:
910	        # calculate the p matrix
911	        p = np.dot(np.linalg.inv(j), np.array([[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1]]))
912	
913	        # calculate the b matrix in terms of cartesian co-ordinates
914	        b = np.transpose(np.dot(np.transpose(b_iso), p))
915	    else:
916	        b = np.zeros((2, 6))  # empty b matrix
917	
918	    return n, b, jacobian
919

926

929	    """

938	            zeta * (2 * zeta - 1),
939	            4 * eta * xi,
940	            4 * xi * zeta,
941	            4 * eta * zeta,
942	        ]
943	    )

1011	def principal_coordinate(
1012	    phi: float,
1013	    x: float,
1014	    y: float,
1015	) -> tuple[float, float]:
1016	    """Converts global coordinates to principal coordinates.
1017	
1018	    Args:
1019	        phi: Principal bending axis angle, in degrees
1020	        x: x-coordinate in the global coordinate system
1021	        y: y-coordinate in the global coordinate system
1022	
1023	    Returns:
1024	        Principal axis coordinates (``x11``, ``y22``)
1025	    """
1026	    phi = phi * np.pi / 180
1027	    cos_phi = np.cos(phi)
1028	    sin_phi = np.sin(phi)
1029	
1030	    return x * cos_phi + y * sin_phi, y * cos_phi - x * sin_phi

1033	def global_coordinate(
1034	    phi: float,
1035	    x11: float,
1036	    y22: float,
1037	) -> tuple[float, float]:
1038	    """Converts prinicpal coordinates to global coordinates.
1039	
1040	    Args:
1041	        phi: Principal bending axis angle, in degrees
1042	        x11: 11-coordinate in the principal coorindate system
1043	        y22: 22-coordinate in the principal coorindate system
1044	
1045	    Returns:
1046	        Global axis coordinates (``x``, ``y``)
1047	    """
1048	    phi = phi * np.pi / 180
1049	    cos_phi = np.cos(phi)

from __future__ import annotations

@dataclass(eq=True, frozen=True)
class Material:
    """Class for structural materials.

    Provides a way of storing material properties related to a specific material. The
    color can be a multitude of different formats, refer to
    https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/colors_api.html and
    https://matplotlib.org/stable/gallery/color/named_colors.html for more information.

    Attributes:
        name: Material name
        elastic_modulus: Material modulus of elasticity
        poissons_ratio: Material Poisson's ratio
        yield_strength: Material yield strength
        density: Material density (mass per unit volume)
        color: Material color for rendering

    Example:
        The following example creates materials for concrete, steel and timber::

            concrete = Material(
                name="Concrete",
                elastic_modulus=30.1e3,
                poissons_ratio=0.2,
                density=2.4e-6,
                yield_strength=32,
                color="lightgrey",
            )
            steel = Material(
                name="Steel",
                elastic_modulus=200e3,
                poissons_ratio=0.3,
                density=7.85e-6,
                yield_strength=500,
                color="grey",
            )
            timber = Material(
                name="Timber",
                elastic_modulus=8e3,
                poissons_ratio=0.35,
                density=6.5e-7,
                yield_strength=20,
                color="burlywood",
            )
    """

    name: str
    elastic_modulus: float
    poissons_ratio: float
    yield_strength: float
    density: float
    color: str

    @property
    def shear_modulus(self) -> float:
        """Returns the shear modulus of the material.

        Material shear modulus, derived from the elastic modulus and Poisson's ratio
        assuming an isotropic material.

        Returns:
            Shear modulus of the material
        """
        return self.elastic_modulus / (2 * (1 + self.poissons_ratio))

## Root cause

In `calculate_geometric_properties` (and `calculate_frame_properties`), the package accumulated the fields documented as ordinary first moments of area with an elastic-modulus weight:

```python
self.section_props.qx += qx * e
self.section_props.qy += qy * e
```

For `DEFAULT_MATERIAL` (E = 1) this coincides with the theory definition `Q_x = ∫y dA`, but for material-bearing models `get_q()` silently returned the modulus-weighted first moments (`E.qx`, `E.qy`) — a different physical quantity with different units — while the supplied theory manual (`paper_assets/theory.rst`) defines first moments of area as unweighted. The elastic-centroid and parallel-axis calculations genuinely need the modulus-weighted moments, but the ordinary first-moment request was conflated with them.

## Fix (generalized, no special-casing)

- `SectionProperties` now stores both quantities: `qx`/`qy` are the ordinary (geometric) first moments of area `∫y dA`, `∫x dA`, and new `eqx`/`eqy` fields hold the modulus-weighted first moments.
- Both geometric analyses accumulate `qx += qx`, `qy += qy` alongside `eqx += qx * e`, `eqy += qy * e`.
- `get_q()` now returns the true ordinary first moments of area for every model, matching the constructed outline.
- Added `get_eq()` to expose the modulus-weighted first moments.
- Elastic-centroid, centroidal-property, and frame-property computations now use `eqx`/`eqy`, so all engineering results (centroids, second moments, warping, stresses, plastic properties) are numerically unchanged.
- `print_results` keeps the original reporting contract: homogeneous sections show `qx`/`qy`, material-bearing sections show the same `E.qx`/`E.qy` weighted values as before.
